title: Serotonin Neurons
intro: All the serotonin (5-HT) in the forebrain comes from a small population of neurons in the raphe nuclei of the brainstem, mostly the dorsal and median raphe. Like dopamine neurons, they are slow pacemakers with enormous, widely branching axons, so a few cells can change the state of the whole cortex. What they signal is less settled than for dopamine; patience, punishment, and the time scale over which rewards are weighed are the leading ideas.

items: Location and numbers: serotonergic cells sit along the midline of the brainstem. The dorsal and median raphe project to the forebrain; caudal raphe groups project to the spinal cord. They number in the tens of thousands in rodents and a few hundred thousand in humans.

Firing: slow and very regular, about 1 to 5 Hz, with broad action potentials, like a clock (Jacobs & Azmitia 1992). Rates are highest in active waking, lower in slow-wave sleep and nearly silent in REM sleep.

Self-inhibition: 5-HT1A autoreceptors on the cells' own somata and dendrites inhibit them when serotonin rises, a negative feedback loop. This is one reason antidepressants that block serotonin reuptake take weeks to act: the autoreceptors must desensitise first.

Receptors: at least 14 receptor subtypes. In cortex, 5-HT1A inhibits and 5-HT2A excites L5 pyramidal cells, and ionotropic 5-HT3 receptors excite a whole family of interneurons (the 5HT3a family, which includes VIP and neurogliaform cells).
Diversity: raphe neurons are heterogeneous; some co-release glutamate (VGLUT3) and groups projecting to different targets differ in inputs and responses.

What they signal: dorsal raphe neurons respond to both reward and punishment, on fast and slow time scales (Cohen, Amoroso & Uchida 2015). Optogenetic activation makes mice wait longer for delayed rewards (Miyazaki et al. 2014; Fonseca, Murakami & Mainen 2015), without being rewarding in itself.
Opponency with dopamine: Daw, Kakade and Dayan (2002) proposed that serotonin reports an aversive, slow prediction error, the opponent of dopamine's appetitive one.

Discount factor: Doya (2002) proposed that neuromodulators set the meta-parameters of reinforcement learning: dopamine the prediction error, serotonin the temporal discount factor (how far ahead rewards count), noradrenaline the exploration temperature and acetylcholine the learning rate. The patience experiments are consistent with this view.
Behavioural inhibition: Dayan and Huys (2008) linked serotonin to stopping actions in the face of predicted punishment, and so to negative mood.
Cellular models: conductance-based models of dorsal raphe neurons reproduce their slow pacemaking, broad spikes and autoreceptor feedback (reviewed in Tuckwell & Penington 2014).

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: A serotonin-like signal is a slow, global scalar that changes a parameter of learning or behaviour (how long the agent waits, how much it weighs future reward) rather than carrying specific content.
In a reward-modulated STDP network you can model it as a second modulator that scales the eligibility trace time constant or the discount factor, alongside the dopamine-like error.
Regular pacemaker firing with autoreceptor feedback is easy to build: an LIF neuron with a bias current and a slow, self-inhibiting current driven by its own output.
